result.title: Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
result.summary: Factual sycophancy, a language model's deference to a user's false beliefs, is usually understood as a bid for the user's approval at the expense of truthfulness. We argue that this framing over-emphasizes the user and propose viewing sycophancy as a failure within the broader and generally useful process of in-context updating, by which models revise their answers based on information supplied during an interaction. We support this view with behavioral and mechanistic evidence. First, models' responses to user claims sit within a broader pattern of source-sensitive updating. They revise their answers in response to information attributed to external sources as well, more so when it appears better supported, and their deference to the user persists even when no user approval is at stake. Second, the internal components that support deference to the user are also causally important for in-context updating more broadly. Our results suggest that factual sycophancy arises when in-context updating gives a user's assertion excessive weight relative to its evidence. Because sycophancy is embedded in this process, reducing it risks reducing useful updating as well, a trade-off that calls for evaluations measuring both behaviors and mitigations that decouple them.

AI.brief_summary: 论文将事实性谄媚重新表述为「上下文更新」失衡：模型会依据来源与证据强度修正答案，且支撑对用户顺从的内部组件对一般上下文更新同样因果重要，因此降低谄媚可能同时削弱有益更新，需同时测量两种行为的评估与解耦式缓解。
